title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
gist: Reacting to the Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, MIT Technology Review's Jessica Hamzelou argues that journalists and investors can never fully verify scientific claims. Theranos's early red flag was missing peer-reviewed data, but peer review itself is fallible (10,000 retractions in 2023) and more and more science now arrives through preprints, press releases and conference talks that skip it.

insights.claim: Theranos, founded by Elizabeth Holmes after she left Stanford in 2003 at age 19, claimed it could run over 100 diagnostic tests on a few drops of blood, raised hundreds of millions of dollars and was valued at $9 billion in 2014, when Forbes put Holmes's worth at $4.5 billion.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Shows how far biotech valuations can run ahead of verified technology when investors rely on founder narrative.

insights.claim: Theranos unraveled after a 2015 Wall Street Journal investigation in which former employees said its tests did not work and samples were run on other companies' machines; Forbes cut Holmes's worth to $0 by 2016, she was charged with fraud in 2018 alongside Ramesh Balwani, and was sentenced in 2022 to a little over 11 years for defrauding investors.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Investigative reporting and whistleblowers, not investor diligence, exposed the fraud, a reminder of where the real verification signal can come from.

insights.claim: Hamzelou says the new documentary You Can See Everything, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, shows Elizabeth Holmes inviting cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe herself as honest, and that she still comes across as an effective manipulator.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Charismatic-founder risk persists even when the facts are known, so sell-side and press credulity remains a recurring diligence hazard.
insights.quote: Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator.
insights.locator: I couldn’t help feeling some empathy

insights.claim: Experienced journalists and insiders were persuaded by Elizabeth Holmes: Fortune's Roger Parloff later said "I blew it," STAT's Matthew Herper wrote that he believes she lied to him, and whistleblower Tyler Shultz said a five-minute conversation could leave him feeling his work was changing the world.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Direct founder access is weak evidence; demand independent data rather than relying on management meetings.

insights.claim: An early red flag at Theranos was the lack of published peer-reviewed data, with much of its work classified as a trade secret.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Biotech companies that cite trade secrecy to avoid publishing core validation data deserve extra skepticism.
insights.quote: One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data.
insights.locator: One of the early red flags

insights.claim: Hamzelou argues peer review cannot be fully trusted: scientists sometimes exaggerate or manipulate data, many findings fail to replicate, and about 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Even published biotech data supporting an investment thesis should be stress-tested for replication.

insights.claim: More and more scientific claims reach the public without peer review through preprint servers such as arXiv, medRxiv and bioRxiv, company press releases, social media and conference presentations, which makes verification harder for journalists.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Market-moving biotech and AI claims increasingly come from unreviewed channels, which raises the risk of narrative-driven mispricing.

insights.claim: Hamzelou says MIT Technology Review does its own informal peer review before publishing new scientific developments, asking trusted outside scientists to assess a claim, but that the Holmes film shows how easily an appealing narrative can still deceive.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Independent expert checks are the practical defense against hype in science-driven sectors.
insights.quote: the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative.
